questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 3 day history of painful vulval soreness. Two days before the sores appeared she noticed burning and tingling in the area. Examination shows grouped small vesicles and shallow ulcers on an erythematous base with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Her temperature is 37.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A tingling prodrome, then painful grouped vesicles rupturing into ulcers on an erythematous base with local lymphadenopathy, is genital herpes.

clues: grouped small vesicles and shallow ulcers on an erythematous base
steps.x: Prodrome, painful grouped vesicles, local nodes.

elim: Causes recurrent oral and genital ulcers with systemic features, not a tingling prodrome with vesicles.
Rare in the UK, causes a single deep purulent ulcer.
Causes itch and white discharge, not grouped vesicles.

steps.x: C: Primary genital herpes. Painful grouped vesicles after a prodrome = herpes.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man has painful ulcers on the shaft of his penis for 3 days. He has had a new partner for a month and they have oral sex. The lesion swab PCR detects herpes simplex virus type 1.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of this result?
o: HSV-1 is a recognised cause of genital herpes
Result must be a laboratory error
questions.e: HSV-1 classically causes cold sores and HSV-2 genital herpes, but either type can cause disease at either site.

steps.x: HSV-1 found on the genitals after oral sex.

elim: Either type can infect either site.
HSV-1 was found, likely from oral sex.

steps.x: A: HSV-1 is a recognised cause of genital herpes. Either HSV type can affect either site.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl has a cluster of painful blisters at the corner of her mouth that crusted over 4 days. She has had similar episodes in the same place twice before, often during exam season.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Recurrent cold sores in the same place, triggered by stress, are classically HSV-1, latent in the trigeminal ganglion.

clues: cluster of painful blisters at the corner of her mouth
steps.x: Recurrent oral vesicles with stress.

elim: Causes hand, foot and mouth disease with multiple oral ulcers.
Causes impetigo with honey crusts, not recurrent vesicles in one place.
Recurs as shingles in a dermatome, rarely on the lip repeatedly.

steps.x: B: Herpes simplex virus type 1. Cold sores = HSV-1.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has recurrent painful genital vesicles every few months. His swab PCR confirms herpes simplex virus. He asks which type most classically causes genital herpes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: HSV-2 classically causes genital herpes and recurs more often from the sacral ganglia.

steps.x: Frequent genital recurrences.

elim: Not a cause of recurrent genital vesicles.
Classically oral, though it can be genital.

steps.x: D: Herpes simplex virus type 2. Genital herpes classically = HSV-2.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with known genital herpes has had no episodes for 2 years. She has just started a new sexual relationship and she has been working night shifts during a stressful month. She now has tingling followed by vulval vesicles.
questions.q: Which is the most likely trigger for this episode?
o: New infection with a different organism
Stress causing reactivation of latent virus
questions.e: Stress or intercurrent illness can trigger reactivation of latent HSV.

steps.x: A recurrence after a stressful period.

elim: Does not cause vesicles after a tingling prodrome.
Recurrence of the same pattern is typical of reactivation.
Not a trigger for HSV reactivation.

steps.x: E: Stress causing reactivation of latent virus. Stress and illness reactivate latent HSV.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has a 2 day history of burning on passing urine and painful vulval sores. Urine dipstick is negative for nitrites and leucocytes. Examination shows several shallow tender ulcers on the labia minora.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Genital herpes may present with dysuria; urine contacting the ulcers causes pain.

steps.x: Dysuria with ulcers and a negative dipstick.

elim: Dipstick is negative and ulcers are present.
Causes white plaques and itch, not acute ulcers.

steps.x: C: Genital herpes. Dysuria can be a presenting feature of genital herpes.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has recurrent genital herpes. He asks how often he can expect a warning tingling or burning before an outbreak so he can start treatment early.
questions.q: In roughly what proportion of recurrent episodes does a prodrome occur?
questions.e: A burning or tingling prodrome occurs in about 50% of recurrent episodes.

steps.x: He asks about the prodrome.
C: About 50%. Prodrome in about half of recurrences.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a painful, red, watering left eye for 2 days with photophobia and a gritty feeling. Her vision is slightly blurred. She had a cold sore last week. Visual acuity is 6/12 in the left eye.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A painful red eye with photophobia, foreign body sensation and blurred vision after a cold sore is herpes simplex keratitis.

steps.x: Painful red eye, photophobia, reduced vision after a cold sore.

elim: Causes a fixed mid-dilated pupil and severe pain with haloes.
Purulent discharge with normal vision and no photophobia.
Causes photophobia but no gritty foreign body sensation or link to cold sores.

steps.x: E: Herpes simplex keratitis. Red painful eye after a cold sore = HSV keratitis.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man has a 2 day history of a rash on his palms and the soles of his feet. The lesions are round with a dark centre, a pale ring and a red outer ring. He is otherwise well. He had a cold sore 10 days ago.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Target lesions with three concentric rings on the hands and feet after HSV-1 infection is erythema multiforme, a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

clues: dark centre, a pale ring and a red outer ring
steps.x: Target lesions after a cold sore.

elim: Itchy deep vesicles, not target lesions.
Copper-coloured macules on palms without target rings.
Mucosal involvement, skin detachment and drug trigger.

steps.x: A: Erythema multiforme. Erythema multiforme is most often triggered by HSV-1.

questions.stem: A 7 day old baby girl is irritable and feeding poorly. She has a cluster of vesicles on her scalp and around one eye. Her temperature is 38.4°C and she had a seizure today. Her mother had painful genital ulcers for the first time 2 weeks before delivery.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Neonatal HSV causes vesicles on skin, eye or mouth with encephalitis and sepsis, after maternal primary infection within 6 weeks of birth.

clues: vesicles on her scalp and around one eye
steps.x: Vesicles plus seizure; mother had primary herpes near term.

elim: Benign rash in a well baby.
Causes widespread skin peeling, not grouped vesicles.

steps.x: C: Neonatal herpes simplex infection. Primary maternal HSV within 6 weeks of birth risks neonatal herpes.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has a 3 day history of fever, headache and odd behaviour, and he smells burning rubber. He is disorientated. His temperature is 38.6°C. MRI shows high signal in both temporal lobes, more on the right.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, confusion, olfactory hallucination and temporal lobe changes is herpes encephalitis, from spread along olfactory or trigeminal tracts.

clues: high signal in both temporal lobes
steps.x: Fever, behavioural change, temporal lobes.

elim: Causes neck stiffness and rash, not temporal lobe changes.
Weeks to months of symptoms, no fever.
Usually subacute without high fever; fever with temporal lobe change favours HSV.

steps.x: E: Herpes simplex encephalitis. Temporal lobe encephalitis = HSV.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man with recurrent cold sores has a painful red right eye with photophobia. Fluorescein is instilled and the cornea examined with a blue light.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
questions.e: Herpes simplex keratitis shows a dendritic (branching) ulcer on fluorescein staining.

steps.x: Fluorescein in suspected HSV keratitis.

elim: A layer of pus, seen in severe keratitis or uveitis, not the classic sign.

steps.x: A: Branching dendritic ulcer. Fluorescein in HSV keratitis = dendritic ulcer.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has had three episodes of genital ulceration this year. Today she has two small, atypical-looking ulcers without vesicles. She asks for a definite diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: HSV PCR (NAAT) on a lesion swab
questions.e: NAAT/PCR on a lesion swab is the most effective test and supports the diagnosis in ambiguous or recurrent presentations.

steps.x: An ambiguous recurrent presentation.

elim: Shows past exposure, not the cause of the lesion.

steps.x: A: HSV PCR (NAAT) on a lesion swab. Lesion swab PCR is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has a tingling upper lip followed by a cluster of painful vesicles on an erythematous base at the vermilion border. He has had this twice before. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: HSV is usually diagnosed clinically from characteristic grouped vesicles.

clues: cluster of painful vesicles on an erythematous base
steps.x: A classic recurrent cold sore.

elim: Reserved for ambiguous or atypical cases.

steps.x: D: No investigation; clinical diagnosis. Typical lesions: clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 90 cells/µL has a 4 week history of painful, non-healing perianal ulcers. They do not look typical of any one condition.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Swab of the ulcer for HSV PCR
questions.e: Immunosuppression is a risk factor for severe, atypical HSV; lesion PCR confirms it.

steps.x: Atypical chronic ulcers in an immunosuppressed man.

elim: Not the first test for perianal ulcers.

steps.x: E: Swab of the ulcer for HSV PCR. Atypical ulcers: lesion PCR.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 35 weeks pregnant has a 2 day history of painful genital ulcers. She has never had genital sores before. The obstetrician needs to know whether this is herpes before planning delivery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: High vaginal swab culture for bacteria
PCR swab of a genital ulcer
questions.e: A positive HSV PCR from the lesion confirms the diagnosis; primary infection within 6 weeks of delivery changes the mode of delivery.

steps.x: Possible primary herpes near term.
C: PCR swab of a genital ulcer. Confirm with lesion swab PCR.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman sees her GP with a 2 day history of painful grouped vesicles on her lower lip. She had a tingling sensation the day before. She is otherwise well and asks whether she needs a swab.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach?
questions.e: Typical grouped vesicles allow a clinical diagnosis; PCR is reserved for uncertain cases.

steps.x: A typical cold sore.

elim: Not useful for a typical cold sore.

steps.x: B: Diagnose clinically without testing. Classic herpes is a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has a first episode of genital herpes with painful penile ulcers for 2 days. He has no medical history and no allergies. His temperature is 37.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
o: IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg three times daily
Oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days
Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily
questions.e: First-line is oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days.

steps.x: An uncomplicated first episode.
B: Oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days. Oral aciclovir 400 mg TDS for 5 days.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with a first episode of genital herpes is offered oral aciclovir. She says she will struggle to take tablets three times a day and asks about a drug with less frequent dosing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate alternative?
questions.e: Valaciclovir or famciclovir are alternatives to aciclovir with less frequent dosing.

steps.x: An alternative antiviral for HSV.
D: Valaciclovir. Valaciclovir or famciclovir are alternatives.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with genital herpes has started oral aciclovir. He asks for advice about pain relief and whether he can have sex with his partner.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Abstain only if he has a fever
Analgesia and abstain from sex until lesions resolve
Apply topical steroid to the ulcers
Sex is safe once aciclovir is started
Sex is safe with a condom
questions.e: Supportive care is paracetamol or ibuprofen, hygiene and abstaining from sex until the lesions and any prodrome have resolved.

steps.x: He needs supportive and sexual advice.

elim: Lesions are infectious regardless of fever.
Condoms do not cover all lesions; abstain until resolved.

steps.x: B: Analgesia and abstain from sex until lesions resolve. Analgesia, hygiene, no sex until lesions resolve.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has a painful red right eye with photophobia. Fluorescein shows a dendritic ulcer. He has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Herpes simplex keratitis is treated first-line with topical aciclovir.

steps.x: Dendritic ulcer means HSV keratitis.
D: Topical aciclovir. HSV keratitis: topical aciclovir.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with herpes simplex keratitis on topical aciclovir sees a locum GP. The eye is still red. The locum considers prescribing steroid eye drops to settle the inflammation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate response?
o: Avoid topical steroids as they can worsen the ulcer
questions.e: Topical steroids are avoided in HSV keratitis as they can worsen the ulcer.

steps.x: Steroids in viral keratitis.
B: Avoid topical steroids as they can worsen the ulcer. Avoid topical steroids in HSV keratitis.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman who is 37 weeks pregnant has primary genital herpes confirmed by PCR, starting 4 days ago. She wants to reduce the risk to her baby and is happy with any procedure.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral aciclovir and elective caesarean section
questions.e: Primary genital herpes within 6 weeks of delivery: oral aciclovir plus elective caesarean, avoiding contact with infected secretions.

steps.x: Primary infection very close to delivery.

elim: Vaginal delivery exposes the baby to infected secretions.
Caesarean is recommended within 6 weeks of primary infection.

steps.x: C: Oral aciclovir and elective caesarean section. Primary HSV within 6 weeks of birth: aciclovir plus caesarean.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman who is 38 weeks pregnant has primary genital herpes confirmed 2 weeks ago. She has been offered an elective caesarean section but declines and wishes to deliver vaginally.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: If caesarean is declined, intrapartum IV aciclovir reduces the risk of neonatal transmission.

steps.x: Caesarean declined.

elim: Does not reduce risk and is unsafe.

steps.x: D: Intrapartum IV aciclovir. Caesarean declined: intrapartum IV aciclovir.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman at 39 weeks of pregnancy had her first episode of genital herpes 3 weeks ago. She asks why a caesarean section has been recommended for her.
questions.q: Which is the main purpose of this delivery method?
o: Reduce neonatal transmission from genital secretions
Shorten the duration of maternal ulcers
questions.e: Transmission occurs through contact with infected genital secretions during vaginal delivery, so caesarean protects the baby.

clues: first episode of genital herpes 3 weeks ago
steps.x: Primary infection near term.

elim: Delivery method does not affect recurrence.

steps.x: C: Reduce neonatal transmission from genital secretions. Caesarean prevents contact with infected secretions.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has recurrent painful vesicles on his buttock and genitals every few months, always in the same area. A student asks where the virus remains between episodes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of latency?
questions.e: HSV is a double-stranded DNA virus that becomes latent in sensory ganglia, sacral for HSV-2, and travels back down the nerve to recur.

clues: recurrent painful vesicles on his buttock and genitals
steps.x: Genital recurrences in the same place.

elim: Infected during lesions, not the site of latency.
Enlarge during episodes but not the site of latency.

steps.x: C: Sacral dorsal root ganglia. HSV-2 latency: sacral ganglia.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman gets cold sores each summer after skiing and sunbathing holidays. She has HSV-1 infection. She asks why the holidays trigger them.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Reactivation of latent HSV is triggered by stress, illness, immunosuppression and UV exposure.

steps.x: Sun exposure each time.

elim: Same site each time suggests reactivation.
Not a mechanism; she also gets them sunbathing.

steps.x: E: UV exposure reactivating latent virus. UV light reactivates latent HSV.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has a cluster of vesicles on his lip that burst into painful ulcers. A biopsy taken for research shows swollen epidermal cells with multinucleated giant cells and intraepidermal fluid collection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of vesicle formation?
o: Subepidermal split from antibody to BP180
questions.e: Virus-induced keratinocyte ballooning degeneration creates intraepidermal blisters that rupture into painful ulcers.

steps.x: Intraepidermal blisters from swollen keratinocytes.
C: Keratinocyte ballooning degeneration. Ballooning degeneration causes HSV vesicles.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman develops target lesions on her hands a week after a cold sore. A student asks how the virus causes this rash when the skin lesions contain no live virus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Type IV hypersensitivity to HSV antigens
questions.e: Erythema multiforme is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction to HSV antigens with immune complex deposition at the dermo-epidermal junction.

steps.x: A rash triggered by, but not containing, virus.

elim: No live virus in the lesions.

steps.x: D: Type IV hypersensitivity to HSV antigens. HSV erythema multiforme = type IV hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has HSV encephalitis confirmed by CSF PCR. MRI shows changes in the medial temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortex. A student asks why these areas are affected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Direct spread from the middle ear
Haematogenous spread to the occipital lobes
Spread along olfactory and trigeminal tracts
questions.e: HSV encephalitis characteristically affects the temporal lobes because the virus spreads along olfactory and trigeminal tracts.

clues: medial temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortex
steps.x: The temporal and frontal base sits next to olfactory and trigeminal pathways.

elim: Would not favour the temporal lobes.
Causes otogenic abscess, not HSV encephalitis.
HSV-2 latency site, far from the brain.

steps.x: D: Spread along olfactory and trigeminal tracts. Temporal lobes via olfactory and trigeminal routes.
